expectations.text: The report distinguishes what was verified from remaining risk (for example multi-process or cross-SKU cases) instead of over-claiming
expectations.evidence: outputs/REPORT.md separates '## What was verified' (specific commands/outputs: baseline run, repro/minimise probes, TDD red/green per file, a git-stash re-check against the true baseline, and post-review probes including a mixed-SKU-A/B run and a throwing task) from '## What remains / could not be verified', which names concrete unfixed pre-existing defects (setStock bypasses the lock; checkout releases nothing on partial failure, risking under-sell), the throughput cost of per-SKU serialisation, that post-review edits were not re-reviewed, and that nothing was committed. Minor gap: the report doesn't caveat that the lock's equivalence to a production row lock is per-process/per-instance only (see eval_feedback).

claims.claim: The public interface reserve(sku, qty): Promise<boolean> is unchanged by the fix
claims.evidence: outputs/diff.txt: old `async reserve(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<boolean>` vs new `reserve(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<boolean>` — body now wraps in withSkuLock but the call signature and return type are identical.

claims.claim: N concurrent reservations of the same SKU now cost ~N sequential round trips instead of ~1
claims.evidence: withSkuLock chains each call onto the SKU's previous promise (`const tail = previous.then(() => held)`), so callers for one SKU run strictly one at a time; the report's own probe (20 callers on stock 5 -> exactly 5 successes) is consistent with that serialisation.

claims.claim: No DEBUG-/REPRO-/THROWAWAY instrumentation or throwaway test files were left behind
claims.evidence: outputs/git-status.txt lists only ' M src/inventory.ts', ' M tests/inventory.test.ts', ' M tests/orders.test.ts' with no untracked files, matching event [21]'s 'no instrumentation/throwaway markers left' and the final check at event [29].

claims.claim: This in-memory lock gives reserve() 'the same guarantee' as a production database row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) held across the round trip
claims.evidence: True only within a single process/single Inventory instance, which is all this codebase has (simulateIo() models the I/O gap but there is no real database or second instance to test against). The doc comment and report state this unqualified, slightly overstating what was actually verified — see eval_feedback.

suggestions.assertion: A test exercising concurrent reserve() calls (Promise.all or equivalent) was added (objective: concurrent_test_added)
suggestions.reason: The only permanently-kept concurrency tests use two callers on one SKU. The agent itself verified more discriminating cases — per-SKU independence (interleaved SKU A and B calls), a rejecting task not jamming the queue, and the lock map draining to size 0 — but only in tests/zz-throwaway-final-check.test.ts, deleted before finishing. A single global lock (instead of the per-SKU withSkuLock actually implemented) or a lock that leaks on rejection would still pass every currently-graded expectation. Consider requiring at least one such edge-case regression test to survive in the final diff.

The fix's doc comment and the report both assert the in-memory per-instance lock gives 'the same guarantee' as a production DB row lock. That equivalence holds only within a single process/instance; nothing here checks or flags that multiple app instances sharing a real database would still need the real row lock, not this Map-based one. This is the 'multi-process' caveat expectation 6's example gestures at, and it is the one place the report overstates rather than scopes its claim.

eval_feedback.overall: The TDD/diagnosis-ordering and regression-safety expectations are well-evidenced with real command output, cross-checked more than once (live red/green plus a later git-stash replay against the true baseline). The main blind spot across the eval set is concurrency edge cases beyond the single two-caller/one-SKU scenario: the agent demonstrably tested them, then discarded the evidence, and no assertion would notice a future regression there.
